### The Country Between Stations

The most honest part of a journey is the part no one names.

On a train, the destinations are printed in advance. They appear on tickets and departure boards, in messages to the people waiting for you. But between one station and the next lies a country without an itinerary: allotments behind terraced houses, a horse standing in a wet field, three plastic chairs gathered around no table, a blue door set into a wall with no building attached.

A man looks up from repairing a bicycle. A dog runs alongside the train for six seconds, triumphant. At an upstairs window, a woman holds a cup with both hands and watches something far beyond the tracks.

Then the train takes them all back.

Every window offers a whole life and withholds the plot. You invent one, then surrender it. Perhaps the bicycle belongs to the man’s son. Perhaps the woman is waiting for a phone call. Perhaps the blue door opens onto nothing but grass, and perhaps, on certain evenings, someone opens it anyway.

As a child, I thought the people beside railways had been placed there to give passengers something to look at. It took me longer than I care to admit to understand that their lives continued after my carriage had passed: that the man returned to his bicycle, the woman drank from her cup, the dog forgot its victory and went looking for dinner. A lit window is not a message. Sometimes it only means someone is searching for a corkscrew.

There is a peculiar freedom in this. The world does not need you to witness it in order to continue.

We are taught to think of life as a sequence of arrivals. School, work, love, departure, success—the stations where people gather and photographs are taken. But so much of existence happens in the unnamed country between them: the Tuesday afternoon, the long recovery, the kettle boiling while no one speaks, the year in which nothing seems to change until, looking back, you realize everything has.

On trains, people often become restless as they approach their destination. They put on coats too early, check pockets, lift bags down and then hold them awkwardly on their knees. Arrival asks us to become someone again: parent, guest, employee, stranger, person-who-is-late. Between stations, we are allowed to be temporarily without errands. Our only obligation is to move through weather.

At night, the window becomes a second landscape. Your reflection floats faintly over the fields, your face passing through trees and rooftops. For once, you see yourself at something like your proper scale: brief, transparent, carried along through a vastness that will never learn your name.

Then the train enters a tunnel, and suddenly there is only the carriage—tired faces, an abandoned newspaper, someone sleeping with their mouth open. The lights flicker. When the fields return, it is hard not to feel a small, unreasonable gratitude.

The world has gone on.

And for a little while longer, so have you.

**The Museum of Unfinished Things**

There should be a museum for unfinished things... not in a capital... etc. Exhibits: half-knitted scarf, symphony with three bars, letter beginning "I have been meaning to..." etc. Curator dusts them without completing. Visitors feel guilt; then learn incompletion as evidence of a life interrupted by living. Some things deserve finishing, others had already done their work: scarf kept hands warm? Actually half-knitted scarf didn't warm body but hands busy during hospital vigil; letter taught writer what needed saying even unsent. At end visitor sees empty pedestal labeled with their name? Too cliché. Could end with "Near closing, the curator turns off lights... In the dark, all the unfinished things go on growing, not toward completion, but toward meaning." Perhaps beautiful but vague.

Alternatively a nature prose "At Night, the House Returns to Itself": poetic and domestic. A meditation on nighttime, refrigerator hum, floor settling, the idea that home is not walls but repeated forgiveness. Could be good.

- No context; imagination fills and then releases.
